# Results — Study 655 (Ivy Portfolio)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test —
Faber's **Ivy Portfolio**: 20% each in US equity (VTI), foreign equity (VEU), REITs (VNQ),
bonds (AGG) and commodities (DBC) captures endowment-style diversification for retail, and an
optional **10-month simple-moving-average timer** applied to each sleeve independently improves
it further — rebuilt on the live-ETF tape. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete
month; the partial current month is dropped; run date 2026-07-10). Fingerprint `6e25c7829c9c`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily auto-adjusted (total-return) closes: **VTI, VEU, VNQ, AGG, DBC** (the five Ivy sleeves) + **BIL** (1-3mo T-bill ETF — cash leg *and* risk-free rate) — public, no key |
| Window | **2007-06-30 → 2026-06-30** (229 months, **19.1 years**) — bound by **BIL's 2007-05-30 inception**, later than VEU (2007-03-08) and DBC (2006-02-06) |
| SMA timer live from | **2008-03-31** (220 months) — 10 months of price history plus the mandatory one-month shift |
| Rebalance | both arms rebalance to target weights **every month** (the natural cadence given monthly data and a monthly SMA re-check); turnover is tracked explicitly at every rebalance |
| Execution / costs | signal from month *t-1*'s close decides the position held during month *t* — exactly **one** lag, no same-bar fills; **5 / 10 bps** one-way × NAV on total absolute weight change per rebalance |
| Sharpe convention | **excess-of-BIL** throughout — static vs 60/40, timed vs static, timed vs 60/40 are all excess-vs-excess races |
| Survivorship | none — five broad, still-listed index/commodity ETFs, not a picked panel |

## The headline — static Ivy (20% × 5) vs 60/40 vs VTI (net, 5 bps)

| leg | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe (excess) | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Ivy static** | +5.70% | 12.89% | **0.392** | **−44.8%** |
| 60/40 (VTI/AGG) | +7.84% | 10.25% | **0.657** | −32.3% |
| VTI buy-and-hold | +10.61% | 16.07% | 0.627 | −50.8% |

| active return | bps/mo | %/yr | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Ivy − 60/40 | −14.1 | −1.69 | −1.12 |
| Ivy − VTI | −41.9 | **−5.03** | **−3.10** |

| bootstrap Sharpe diff (2,000 resamples, 6-mo blocks) | point | 95% CI | share arm A wins |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Ivy − 60/40 | **−0.265** | **[−0.470, −0.018]** | 1.7% |
| Ivy − VTI | −0.234 | [−0.434, +0.003] | 2.8% |

The core "endowment diversification" claim does **not** survive contact with 2007–2026 data.
Ivy's risk-adjusted profile is **robustly worse than a plain 60/40** — the bootstrap 95% CI of
the Sharpe gap sits entirely below zero, stable across block sizes (3/6/12 months all give a
negative CI) — and it also lags VTI's raw return by a HAC-certified −5.03%/yr. Its drawdown
(−44.8%) is worse than 60/40's (−32.3%) and only marginally better than 100% equities (−50.8%).

## Why: two of the five legs were themselves disasters on this sample

| leg | CAGR | Sharpe (excess) | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| VTI (US equity) | +10.61% | 0.627 | −50.8% |
| VEU (foreign equity) | +5.00% | 0.289 | −58.4% |
| VNQ (REITs) | +5.40% | 0.291 | **−64.6%** |
| AGG (bonds) | +3.06% | 0.385 | −17.1% |
| DBC (commodities) | **+1.33%** | **0.096** | **−74.6%** |

DBC (commodities) returned almost nothing over 19 years with a Sharpe near zero and its own
−75% drawdown — commodity index funds paid a well-documented negative roll yield through the
2011–2020 bear market. VNQ (REITs) crashed −64.6% in its own right and moved *with* equities,
not against them, in the 2008 crisis. Diversification only helps when the diversifiers have
decent risk/return profiles of their own; two of Faber's five didn't, on this tape.

## The 10-month SMA overlay — timed vs static, same 220-month window

| leg | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe (excess) | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Ivy static (this window) | +5.87% | 13.02% | 0.411 | −44.8% |
| 60/40 (this window) | +8.43% | 10.36% | 0.716 | −29.9% |
| **Ivy TIMED (10-mo SMA)** | +4.67% | **6.87%** | 0.520 | **−13.3%** |

Drawdown ratio timed/static = **0.30**; timed/60-40 = **0.44**.

| active return | bps/mo | %/yr | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| timed − static | −14.7 | −1.77 | −0.79 |
| timed − 60/40 | −32.0 | **−3.84** | **−2.26** |

| bootstrap Sharpe diff | point | 95% CI | share timed wins |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| timed − static | +0.109 | [−0.240, +0.414] | 68.4% |
| timed − 60/40 | −0.196 | [−0.589, +0.166] | 13.5% |

The drawdown cut is dramatic and mechanical (−44.8% → −13.3%): the timer works as a crash
shield. It does **not** work as a return engine — CAGR is worse than static Ivy (not
significant, *t* = −0.79) and **significantly worse than 60/40** (−3.84%/yr, HAC *t* = −2.26).
The Sharpe point estimate improves over static Ivy (+0.109) but the bootstrap CI still spans
zero — not certified — and timed Ivy's Sharpe never catches 60/40's on this tape either.

## Sub-period — is this one great sidestep (2008 alone)?

Ex-GFC (drop 2007-07 → 2009-06):

| leg | CAGR | Sharpe | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Ivy static ex-GFC | +8.06% | 0.644 | −19.3% |
| 60/40 ex-GFC | +10.05% | **0.924** | −20.6% |
| Ivy timed ex-GFC | +5.78% | 0.673 | **−13.1%** |
| Ivy static ex-GFC (timed window) | +8.23% | 0.660 | −19.3% |

Active Ivy − 60/40 ex-GFC: **−1.68%/yr** (HAC *t* = −1.33). Active timed − static ex-GFC:
**−2.68%/yr** (*t* = −1.92). Active timed − 60/40 ex-GFC: **−4.32%/yr** (*t* = −2.78).

Two honest readings, both hold with 2008 removed: (1) the static-diversification underperformance
vs 60/40 is **not** a 2008 artefact — it persists ex-GFC, just below the certification bar; (2)
the timer's drawdown cut is **not** a one-time 2008 sidestep either — it still shrinks max
drawdown by a third (−19.3% → −13.1%) with the crash removed, so the timing mechanism is doing
real, repeated work across the sample, not living off one great trade.

## Costs and turnover — cheap to hold, not cheap to time

One-way bps × NAV on the total absolute weight change at every monthly rebalance.

| arm | turnover | cost drag (5 bps) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Ivy static | **28%/yr** | negligible |
| Ivy timed | **361%/yr** (8.89 sleeve-flips/yr across 5 legs) | ≈ 18 bps/yr |

| timed, cost sweep | CAGR | Sharpe | max DD |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps | +4.67% | 0.520 | −13.3% |
| 10 bps | +4.49% | 0.494 | −13.4% |

Costs are a rounding error either way — the static leg trades almost nothing, and even the
timer's ~9 flips/year across five sleeves costs only ~18–36 bps/yr. **Costs are not why this
underperforms 60/40; the legs and the timing trade-off are.**

## Third axis — does the SMA carry real timing information, or just less exposure?

Matched-exposure random-timing control: for each of the five sleeves, shuffle its in/out
calendar at random while holding its **time-in-market fixed** — same average exposure, random
*when*. Averaged over **40 seeds** (single-seed baselines are banned on this desk).

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| actual timed Sharpe / max DD | **0.520 / −13.3%** |
| random-timing baseline (mean) | Sharpe 0.372 / max DD −32.3% |
| actual beats on drawdown | **100% of 40 shuffles** |
| actual beats on Sharpe | **95% of 40 shuffles** (38/40) |

The 10-month rule is not merely "less time in the market" — a matched-exposure random timer
gets nowhere close to the same protection. This is genuine, if partial, trend information, not
an artefact of reduced average exposure.

## Synthetic machinery control — the detector is faithful

A deterministic monthly 5-asset + cash world where a single regime drives all five legs with a
TUNABLE ``persistence`` knob; unconditional means (persistence=0, i.e. a fair 50/50 coin flip)
are pinned at realistic positive asset premia **above** the cash rate in every world, so hiding
in cash can never mechanically win — only genuine trend information can. The same
matched-exposure random-timing test is applied inside the synthetic world, averaged over
**10 world-seeds × 20 inner shuffle-seeds** each.

| world | mean Sharpe-beat-share | mean DD-beat-share |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (persistence = 0.00) | **49.5%** (chance = 50%) | 69.5% |
| planted (persistence = 0.85) | **75.0%** | 82.5% |

The Sharpe-beat-share sits at chance under the null and rises cleanly once a trend is planted —
the timing detector is unbiased. The null's DD-beat-share (69.5%, above the 50% chance line) is
a named, honest artefact: **any** trailing-average rule mechanically tends to have already
de-risked once a run of bad recent returns has occurred, capping further downside somewhat even
with zero informational content — a structural property of trend-following, not skill. The real
tape's beat-shares (100% / 95%) exceed even the planted-0.85 world, consistent with 2007–2026
containing one genuinely strong, sustained trend episode (the GFC) plus smaller ones — not proof
of an unusually powerful timer. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support
of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** *Real on the SMA timer's drawdown cut* (−44.8% → −13.3%, validated
  against a matched-exposure random-timing control — beats 100%/40 shuffles on drawdown, 95%/40
  on Sharpe — and against the synthetic null/planted control) **·** *None on the static 5-asset
  diversification's promise of a better risk-adjusted mix than 60/40* (bootstrap 95% CI of the
  Sharpe gap sits entirely below zero: [−0.470, −0.018]; CAGR and drawdown both trail 60/40 too).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Cheap to run either way (turnover 28%/yr static, 361%/yr timed;
  costs a rounding error, ≤36 bps/yr) — but nothing survives to trade: static Ivy's Sharpe is
  robustly worse than a free 60/40, and timed Ivy's much-improved drawdown never converts into a
  certified Sharpe edge over 60/40 either (CI [−0.589, +0.166]) while its return is
  significantly worse (HAC *t* = −2.26). You are not paid to run this over the boring benchmark.
- **"Risk reduction or alpha (the 10-month SMA)?" — CONFIRMED (risk reduction, not alpha).**
  The drawdown protection is real, repeated (survives ex-GFC), and validated against both a
  matched-exposure random-timing control and a synthetic positive control. The return cost is
  also real — timed Ivy significantly underperforms 60/40 in raw return (*t* = −2.26) — exactly
  Faber's own framing of the trade-off, now shown to hold across a 5-asset composite, not just
  the single-asset case (Study 110).
